705.bp: When you buy things online or move money through a bank, the system remembers every action you take—every click, every purchase, every login. Traditionally, systems learned patterns from the order these actions happened in (like: you searched for shoes, then looked at reviews, then bought). But they miss something crucial: the hidden connections between you and the items. If millions of other people bought the same shoes, that shared interest is a signal the system throws away.
705.wh: The tension is this: order-based learning (what happened first, second, third) is great at spotting sequences, but it ignores the big web of who-bought-what-together. Meanwhile, treating the web structure separately from the sequence loses the timing—when did the connection form? Both pieces of information matter, but existing methods force you to pick one.
705.ww: When you mix the two—the order of your actions AND the web of connections—the system can spot when you're similar to someone you've never directly interacted with, just by recognizing that you both connect to the same things in the same order. It's like the system becomes a detective: instead of only looking at your personal diary, it also checks 'oh, I see you're connected to Item X, and so are 500 other people who then bought Item Y. You probably will too.'
705.ap: The authors propose three specific ways to weave in the connection-web structure: first, they enrich the sequence embeddings themselves by mixing in signals about the graph; second, they directly align your learned profile with your position in the web; third, they add a training task that explicitly teaches the model to predict graph structure. They test which strategy works best depending on how connected the graph is.
705.po: On real financial and e-commerce data, this mixed approach improved fraud detection and recommendation accuracy by up to 2.3 percentage points. The research also reveals that how connected the graph is matters: dense graphs (where everything touches everything) favor one strategy; sparse graphs favor another.

706.bp: Question-and-answer platforms like Stack Overflow or Korean Knowledge iN let people post questions and get answers from the public. For decades this worked because real humans answered—they drew on experience, lived through problems, could explain nuance. Now, AI language models can generate answers that sound plausible and often correct. The question is not 'can the AI fool us?' but 'how is this changing the platform's soul? Are humans still the backbone, or are we gradually replacing them?'
706.wh: The hard part is that AI-generated answers look nearly identical to human answers in the raw text. Humans don't wear a uniform. An AI might write longer, use more punctuation, reuse similar phrases; but so might a human with that style. You need to detect the subtle fingerprints that only AI leaves—patterns in word choice, structure, even the probability of certain words appearing together.
706.ww: Language models are trained on massive amounts of text data, which biases them toward certain patterns that real humans (especially Q&A answerers) use less frequently. For example, humans ramble; they use conversational filler; they sometimes contradict themselves. AI models are smoother, more formal, more consistent—not because they're better, but because they're sampling from a learned probability distribution that's been squeezed into a matrix of numbers. These statistical fingerprints are learnable.
706.ap: The researchers implemented nine existing AI-detection methods (each one looks for different fingerprints: word distributions, syntax patterns, semantic consistency, etc.). They stacked the three best-performing ones together, using the outputs of each as inputs to a final classifier. On real Q&A platform data, this ensemble detector achieved 99.87% accuracy.
706.po: Using this detector, they found 75,558 AI-generated answers among 1.46 million. Interestingly, these AI answers received the same upvote/downvote reaction as human answers, suggesting people can't tell the difference. But AI answers tend to be longer and more diverse in language. The real surprise: the platform is shifting—questions are moving away from 'what are the facts?' toward 'what's your personal story?'—territory where humans still have the edge.

707.bp: Rainfall forecasting saves lives. When a storm is coming, water managers need to know if it'll rain, when, and how hard, so they can release water from dams, evacuate people, and manage infrastructure. Modern AI models trained on weather data can make these predictions, but they face a strange problem: rain doesn't fall every day, and the model doesn't know how to predict 'no rain'—it predicts a tiny amount of drizzle everywhere instead.
707.wh: Most modern time-series foundation models (large pre-trained models that predict numbers over time) assume the output is a smooth, continuous curve. They're built for things like temperature or stock prices, which follow that pattern. But rain is different: on any given day, there's a discrete decision (rain yes/no), and only if yes, how much. These models output continuous numbers, so they can't represent the true zero-or-something structure. Retraining these massive models for this specific case would cost thousands of dollars and tons of electricity.
707.ww: The insight is: you don't need to retrain the model. Instead, post-process its predictions. The model outputs a number for each day (say, 2.3mm when it won't actually rain). You can then ask: 'what percentage of days in history had zero rain?' Then you can mathematically map the model's predictions to either truly-zero (no rain) or positive-value (it will rain), using statistical tools that preserve the overall pattern the model learned.
707.ap: They apply three mathematical corrections in sequence: first, they use historical rain-probability to restore the true zero mass (days with no rain); second, they use a probability-integral transform to align the distribution of rainy days; third, they apply a tail-mapping technique for extreme storms. Each step takes the model's predictions and reshapes them to match reality's actual structure.
707.po: On South Australian rainfall data, this wrapper dramatically reduced false alarms (drizzle predictions) and improved detection of actual storms, with almost zero computational cost (5 milliseconds per forecast vs. hundreds of GPU-hours for retraining). The method is so cheap and general that it can be deployed globally without retraining.

708.bp: Imagine a social network that changes over time: new people join, new groups form, and friendships shift. Now imagine the network is so large that you can't retrain the model from scratch every time something changes. You need a system that learns on-the-fly while remembering what it learned before. The challenge is common in real platforms—your knowledge model was trained last month, but today's graph looks different, with new categories of people and new connection patterns.
708.wh: The tension is two-fold. First, when new kinds of people appear (new classes), the model struggles to categorize them because they're completely foreign. Second, when the features of existing people change (someone's style, interests, or behavior shift), the model forgets its old knowledge trying to fit the new pattern—called catastrophic forgetting. You can't solve both at once: if you prioritize learning the new, you lose the old; if you stay rigid about the old, you fail on the new.
708.ww: The breakthrough idea: separate the unchanging core from the changeable surface. Each person has a 'semantic' part (their true category—are they a tech person? social person? whatever the fixed categories are) and a 'domain' part (their current style—how they dress in this time period, how they speak now). When the style changes, only the style part should update; the core stays put. This way, when you see a new style, you recognize the core is still the same, so you don't forget.
708.ap: DINGLE has two modules. The first breaks apart a person's learned profile into these two pieces (semantic core + current style), using a neural decoupler. The second uses a teacher-student setup where the teacher model guards the old knowledge and the student learns new patterns; knowledge flows from teacher to student, preventing forgetting. They also keep banks of example representations and model parameters to make sure old knowledge doesn't evaporate.
708.po: On five real-world graph datasets, DINGLE improved classification accuracy while successfully learning new classes without forgetting old ones. It beat eleven other methods that tried to solve either the class problem or the domain problem separately.

709.bp: This is an announcement, not a research paper: Samsung's research team is hosting a workshop to discuss where web advertising is headed. The field is under pressure—regulators want privacy, companies want personalization, users want good experiences, and all three are in tension. The workshop exists to bring these worlds together and imagine solutions.
709.wh: The friction is unavoidable: every ad targeted to you relies on knowing something about you, which raises privacy alarms. AI can help personalize without tracking, but that's still emerging. Meanwhile, new immersive technologies (VR, AR, interactive ads) are arriving faster than we have ethical frameworks for them.
709.ww: No single company or research group can solve this alone. You need advertising engineers, privacy specialists, data scientists, and ethicists talking to each other. Often they speak past each other—privacy people say 'block all tracking,' advertising people say 'tracking is how we work,' and the truth lives in the middle. Workshops create spaces where that dialogue can happen.
709.ap: Samsung is creating a forum where researchers and practitioners from different fields present cutting-edge work, discuss challenges, and collectively explore solutions at the intersection of privacy, AI, and user experience.
709.po: The workshop aims to influence the future of web advertising: shaping it toward ethical standards, responsible AI use, and privacy-respecting personalization. It's a platform for research and ideas to flow from academia into industry practice.

710.bp: Video platforms like Kuaishou serve billions of searches every day—people looking for short clips on every topic imaginable. But many searches are for niche topics (long-tail queries) where few people have searched before, so the platform has little data on what videos users found satisfying. The result: low-quality content (clickbait, shallow videos) rises to the top because algorithms only have sparse interaction signals to learn from. The goal is to surface genuinely good content even when almost nobody's clicked on it yet.
710.wh: The fundamental tension: you want to rank videos by true quality (would users enjoy this?), but you only have clicks and views—sparse, noisy, biased signals that favor sensational content. If a niche video is excellent but hasn't been discovered yet, the algorithm will bury it. Retraining a ranking model from scratch is expensive; you need a faster lever.
710.ww: Large language models already have learned vast amounts about the world and about video content. They've been trained on billions of text descriptions, reviews, and discussions. This means an LLM can independently assess whether a video is shallow clickbait or genuinely informative, without ever seeing who clicked on it. It's like having a critic who doesn't know the popularity numbers—just the content itself.
710.ap: The authors build a two-stage system: stage one uses multimodal evidence (video frames, text, audio) to create training data about which videos are high-quality, using an LLM to assign these labels. Stage two uses preference-learning (the model learns that video A is better than video B) to fine-tune the ranking. At serving time, the learned quality scores rerank videos and feed into reinforcement learning for page-level optimization.
710.po: In offline tests, this improved ranking quality (AUC, diversity metrics). In a live A/B test on 15% of real traffic, users watched more videos and reported higher satisfaction—all while the system promoted higher-quality but previously-underexposed content. The Matthew effect (rich-get-richer) was partially reversed.

711.bp: Pathologists examine tissue samples under microscopes to diagnose disease. For each image, they must mark regions of interest—tumor, normal, inflamed tissue—pixel by pixel. This is exhausting and error-prone. Modern computer vision models could automate this, but training them requires thousands of hand-drawn pixel-level masks from experts. Creating these takes weeks of manual work. The question is: can we train a model with only image-level labels (doctors just say 'this tissue is cancerous') instead of pixel-level labels, cutting annotation time from weeks to hours?
711.wh: Weakly-supervised segmentation has a fundamental problem: without pixel-level truth, the model struggles to distinguish between what's actually tumor and what's just background coincidence. Two challenges make this worse: tissues of the same type look different (intra-class variation—tumor cells don't all look identical), and different tissue types can look similar (inter-class confusion—inflamed tissue might look like early tumor). The model easily gets confused and latches onto spurious patterns rather than true diagnostic features.
711.ww: If you pair the vision model with a language model (which has been trained on medical descriptions), the language model becomes a critic. When the vision model is unsure ('is this tissue A or B?'), the language model can provide semantic guidance ('tissue A is characterized by these features'). By making the vision model's learned features match the language model's textual descriptions, you ground the pixel-level predictions in real medical knowledge rather than accident.
711.ap: The method uses hierarchical text prompts: for each tissue class, they create text descriptions and embed them using a pre-trained language model. The vision model learns to align its features at multiple layers with these text embeddings. They also use hierarchical class prompts, where each class is subdivided into clusters (subtypes) to capture internal variation. High-confidence predictions from this process become pseudo-labels (guesses) for further training.
711.po: On histopathology datasets, this weakly-supervised approach generated pixel-level segmentations that rival full supervision, without requiring experts to hand-draw masks for thousands of images. The method captures both fine-grained details and coarse structure, improving diagnostic accuracy while slashing annotation burden.

712.bp: ChatGPT now has a memory feature: it remembers things you tell it across conversations. You might mention your dog's name, your job title, or your health concerns in one chat, and the system recalls these in the next week's conversation. This personalization is powerful—the system feels like it knows you. But it also creates a hidden profile: a data portrait of who you are, built from your casual disclosures. The question is: who controls this portrait, and what's in it?
712.wh: The core tension: personalization requires remembering facts about you, but facts about health, finances, family, or beliefs are sensitive. Users don't always realize they're being profiled when they chat. They assume they're having private conversations, not that their words are being extracted and stored as structured data. And they have little visibility into what the system 'remembered' or how it was used.
712.ww: A memory is only useful if it's accurate and relevant. If the system misunderstands what you said and stores a false 'fact,' you've been mislabeled. If it correctly extracts sensitive details but uses them to infer private information (like health status from casual mentions), you've been profiled without consent. Transparency lets users see what's happening and correct errors.
712.ap: The researchers analyzed 2,050 real memory entries from 80 ChatGPT users. They classified what each memory contained: structured facts (dog name, job), personal data under GDPR (address, financial status), or psychological insights (personality traits, fears). They also checked whether the system created the memory or the user explicitly asked for it. Then they designed Attribution Shield, a tool that alerts users to sensitive inferences and suggests safer ways to phrase the same idea.
712.po: Key findings: 96% of memories were created unilaterally by the system (users didn't ask); 28% contained GDPR-defined personal data; 52% contained psychological inferences. 84% were accurate. Attribution Shield demonstrates that you can show users what's happening and protect them without losing personalization—it's a middle ground between total transparency and privacy.

713.bp: Imagine you're asked: 'Who won the 2024 Olympics, and what sport did they represent at university?' This requires hopping through multiple facts: find the winner, find their background, verify their sport. Traditional search engines would ask you to do this manually (search, click, search again, click). New AI systems promise to answer multi-hop questions in one step by retrieving relevant information and synthesizing it. But they often break down mid-way: they make a wrong guess at one step, and the subsequent steps cascade off a cliff.
713.wh: The challenge is error propagation. If the system misunderstands the first question ('who won?'), the second search will be for the wrong person entirely. Additionally, language models are prone to decomposing complex questions incorrectly—they might miss which parts are questions and which parts are constraints. There's no way to recover from these early mistakes, so the final answer is nonsense.
713.ww: The key insight: structure the question into an explicit tree before you start searching. Instead of letting the model freestyle its search path, force it to create a plan: 'the core question is X, these are the known entities (facts I already have), these are the unknown entities (facts I need to find).' This tree acts as a roadmap. If the model strays, you catch it. More importantly, when you're traversing the tree bottom-up, each level is constrained by the level below it, so errors don't cascade as badly.
713.ap: Reasoning Tree Guided RAG (RT-RAG) builds an explicit reasoning tree by parsing the question for entities and constraints, using consensus voting to pick the best tree from multiple candidates. Then it traverses the tree bottom-up, searching for and refining information at each step. When the model rewrites a query for the next search, it grounds the rewrite in the evidence found so far, preventing drift.
713.po: On multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, RT-RAG improved performance by 7.0 percentage points in exact match and 6.0 points in F1 score compared to methods that let the model freestyle its reasoning. The structured approach trades flexibility for reliability.

714.bp: Watch a live stream on your phone, and packets are traveling across cellular networks—WiFi, 4G, 5G—each prone to dropping data. If a packet is lost, the video frame is corrupted; if too many frames corrupt, the stream stutters and becomes unwatchable. Real-time video (sports, gaming, live news) is especially sensitive: a one-second delay destroys the experience. The goal is to deliver video without stutters even when the network is unreliable, while using the minimum necessary bandwidth.
714.wh: The classic solution is Forward Error Correction (FEC): send extra redundant packets so the receiver can recover from loss. But how much redundancy is enough? Too little, and you still get stutters; too much, and you waste bandwidth. Most systems apply the same FEC level to every frame, missing a crucial fact: loss doesn't happen uniformly. Sometimes the network loses three packets in a row (burst loss), but the system protected each frame independently, wasting protection on frames that weren't hit.
714.ww: Burst loss is the key insight: a burst of packet loss at the network level can affect multiple frames, but the damage can be smoothed out if you protect at a multi-frame level rather than per-frame. Imagine frames A, B, C and the network loses two packets in a row. If FEC protected A and B separately, both would be damaged. But if FEC protected A+B+C as a unit, the burst hits hard locally but the recovery algorithm can stitch everything back together from the redundancy in the group.
714.ap: Breath dynamically adjusts the 'protection boundary'—the grouping of frames under one FEC umbrella—based on real-time network conditions and video properties. When burst loss is expected (e.g., network congestion detected), it widens the boundary (group more frames); when loss is sparse, it narrows the boundary (use less redundancy). The system continuously adapts based on observed packet loss patterns and video bitrate.
714.po: In emulated mobile networks with real production traffic, Breath reduced video playback interruptions by 17-22% and allowed higher video bitrate (10-14% improvement) compared to fixed-boundary FEC schemes. The adaptive approach trades real-time computation for better user experience and bandwidth efficiency.

715.bp: You visit a news website, and without you knowing, an invisible 1x1 pixel image loads from a third-party server (advertisers, data brokers, etc.). That tiny image exfiltrates information: your IP address, browser cookies, the page you're on. This happens across thousands of websites, building a profile of your behavior across the internet. Unlike cookies, pixel tracking is stealthy and cheap. Defense tools like ad blockers struggle because pixels hide in plain sight, looking like legitimate content.
715.wh: Detecting pixel tracking is hard because the network traffic looks legitimate—it's just an HTTP request for an image, indistinguishable from a real image load. You can't block all image requests; the site's content won't load. You need to understand the context: is this image request truly needed for the page to display, or is it harvesting data? This requires understanding associations across websites—if server X appears as an invisible tracker on 1,000 sites, it's probably malicious, even if it looks normal in isolation.
715.ww: The solution is to model the problem as a graph: websites are nodes, and requests between them are edges. If you can learn which edges are tracking (third-party associations that harvest data) and which are legitimate, you can build a model of the tracking infrastructure. Large language models have already learned what legitimate vs. deceptive third parties typically look like (from their training data), so you can use them to label initial examples, then train a specialized detection model on that labeled data.
715.ap: TGNN (Tracking Graph Neural Network) encodes HTTP traffic into quadruples (domain, path, resource, destination), then models the cross-site associations as a directed graph (Tracking Directed Graph). It uses a graph neural network to learn both semantic features (what does the request contain?) and interaction patterns (which combinations are suspicious?). To overcome label scarcity, they use an LLM with minimal expert input to generate high-quality labels automatically.
715.po: On traffic from the top 10,000 websites, TGNN detected pixel tracking with high accuracy, outperforming existing filter-list and machine-learning baselines. The measurement revealed that at least 16.74% of websites use pixel tracking via major third-party services, establishing cross-site tracking as widespread infrastructure rather than fringe abuse.

716.bp: Advertisers run campaigns with fixed budgets—spend 10,000 dollars over a month. But ad auctions change minute-to-minute: sometimes ad space is cheap, sometimes expensive. An advertiser wants to spread their 10,000 dollars evenly across the month so they don't burn it all in one expensive day and run out later. This is called 'budget pacing'—controlling the spend rate to match the campaign goal.
716.wh: The standard approach is ad-hoc parameter tuning: adjust dials until the spend rate looks right. But auctions are chaotic; a parameter that works today might overshoot or undershoot tomorrow. If you spend too fast early, you run out of budget when the best inventory arrives later. If you spend too slow, you waste the opportunity. You need a controller that automatically adjusts to changing auction conditions without manual fiddling.
716.ww: Control theory—the math behind thermostats and cruise control—offers a proven framework. Instead of tuning parameters manually, set a desired spend rate, measure the actual spend rate, and feed the error (desired minus actual) back into an adjustment mechanism. Over time, the system self-corrects. Crucially, adding a bit of 'hysteresis' (don't react to every tiny fluctuation) prevents oscillation—overshooting one way, then correcting too hard the other way.
716.ap: The authors propose a controller combining hysteresis (thresholds that must be crossed before reacting) with proportional feedback (the size of the correction is proportional to the error). For a budget campaign, the controller tracks the desired spend rate and adjusts bidding behavior to stay on track. They provide analysis for parameter selection so practitioners can tune it correctly for their auction environment.
716.po: In real online auctions, this control-theoretic approach reduced pacing error by 13% and reduced volatility in spending by 54% compared to existing methods. It's particularly valuable for small-budget campaigns where overshoot is disastrous; the principled approach is far more stable than manual tuning.

717.bp: Intelligent tutoring systems track what students have learned as they progress through a course. If the system knows whether a student has mastered algebra, geometry, and calculus, it can recommend the right next problem. This is knowledge tracing. But students take courses across multiple disciplines (math, then physics, then computer science), and knowledge in one discipline helps in another. A student who masters algebra finds physics easier. The challenge is: how do you transfer learning across disciplines when knowledge structures are different?
717.wh: The tension is two-fold: students have different cognitive abilities (some are natural problem-solvers, others are memorizers), which shift as they move between disciplines. Additionally, disciplines organize knowledge differently—algebra focuses on symbolic manipulation, physics on conceptual models, computer science on logic. A model trained on algebra students might not work for physics students, even if they're learning similar underlying concepts.
717.ww: The key insight: separate the 'what' from the 'how.' Every discipline has meta-skills—deep cognitive patterns that transcend subjects (reasoning, pattern-matching, abstraction). These transcend disciplines. What changes is the domain-specific surface: how you express your reasoning in symbols vs. diagrams vs. code. If you can extract and align these meta-skills, you can transfer learning across disciplines even if the content looks different.
717.ap: DTransKT has two modules. The Cross-disciplinary Graph-matching (CG) module extracts meta-skill representations from each student's learning trajectory, then aligns these across disciplines. The Cross-disciplinary Attention-assisting (CA) module uses a pre-trained language model to extract meta-semantics from textual course content, so knowledge from one discipline can inform another. These components work together to make a knowledge-tracing model work across multiple subjects.
717.po: When applied to seven existing knowledge-tracing models, DTransKT improved transfer-learning accuracy by 14.2% on average and improved AUC by 4.5%. The framework enables a single system to track student progress across math, science, and humanities—traditionally siloed domains—without retraining from scratch for each new discipline.

718.bp: Recommendation systems learn from user behavior: you click videos, so the system shows you similar videos. But noise corrupts this signal—you might click something by accident, or one bad click shouldn't outweigh ten good ones. The system should amplify strong signals (this user genuinely loves this type of content) and suppress noise (random clicks, clickbait). The challenge is especially hard when data is sparse: what if very few people have interacted with an item? You're making recommendations in the dark.
718.wh: Graph-based recommendation systems face two opposing problems: random edge perturbations (used to train the model) can accidentally delete the strongest signal edges, teaching the model noise. Meanwhile, sparse data means you have few edges to learn from anyway, so the model generalizes poorly. You need augmentation (creating training variation) that's smart enough to preserve true signals while filtering noise.
718.ww: Instead of random perturbation, use a learned denoising process: imagine gradually adding noise to the graph until it's chaos, then learning to remove that noise step-by-step. A model trained on this diffusion process learns which edges are robust (survive noise) and which are fragile (noise). Real user-preference edges are typically robust. This diffusion-based augmentation is far smarter than random erasure.
718.ap: RaDAR combines two mechanisms: a generative model that captures the global structure of the user-item graph, and a denoising model that refines noisy edges. It uses asymmetric comparisons (learning from mismatches of different weights) with global negative sampling to maintain semantic consistency. The relation-aware component dynamically adjusts edge importance based on learned node semantics, not fixed rules.
718.po: On three real recommendation benchmarks, RaDAR outperformed existing methods, especially on noisy and sparse datasets. The diffusion-guided augmentation and relation-aware refinement both contributed to robustness—the system made better recommendations even when user behavior data was incomplete or contradictory.

719.bp: When you watch a video, pause, then continue later, the recommendation system should remember where you were and suggest what's likely to come next. This is sequential recommendation—understanding that users have an evolving interest over time, not a static preference. The system learns patterns: people who watch intro tutorials then advanced tutorials then project examples tend to learn well. The challenge is capturing this evolution without forcing the model to memorize individual sequences.
719.wh: Most methods use fixed data augmentation (random shuffling, dropout) to create training variations. But these are blunt instruments: shuffling might destroy the very sequence pattern you're trying to learn. And there's no guarantee that the augmented version preserves what the user actually cares about—their intent. If a user watches cooking tutorials then physics lectures, random augmentation might create a fake 'user' who does the opposite order, confusing the model about what sequences are valid.
719.ww: Instead of predefined augmentation, learn which perturbations are valid. A learnable perturbation network learns what changes in a sequence are acceptable (watching videos in a different order is fine, but completely changing genres might not be). A restoration network then learns to recover the essential user intent from the perturbed sequence. Together, they generate semantically valid variations that preserve what truly matters.
719.ap: ACLSRec (Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Sequential Recommendation) trains two neural networks jointly: one that perturbs (changes) user sequences in learnable ways, and one that restores (recovers the original intent). The model uses these networks to generate augmented versions of sequences during training, then learns from pairs of original and augmented sequences. This adaptive augmentation is specific to each user and dataset.
719.po: On real e-commerce and entertainment datasets, ACLSRec achieved higher recommendation accuracy than fixed-augmentation baselines. By preserving semantic consistency across augmented views, the model learned more robust interest patterns and made better predictions about what users would watch or buy next.
